q.sub_topic: The stage of researching and booking guests
q.question: Researching the topic, booking the guests and writing the rundown belong to which stage of TV production?
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pre-production
Why: All planning done before the recording, such as research, booking guests and scripting, is pre-production.
Why not the others: (A) is the recording itself. (C) is the work done after recording, such as editing. (D) concerns delivering the programme to viewers.
Key point: Most of a talk show's quality is decided in pre-production.

q.sub_topic: The list of segments with their timings
q.question: The document that lists each segment of the show with its exact timing is called the:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Rundown
Why: A rundown (running order) sets out the sequence and length of every segment, so that the show runs to time.
Why not the others: (A) shows shots as drawings. (B) tells the crew when to report. (C) is a short summary.
Key point: Live and studio shows are run from the rundown.

q.sub_topic: Why the studio uses three cameras
options: A) Different angles are captured and shown as people speak
B) It removes the need to edit the programme afterwards
C) It allows the show to be shot without any lights
D) It means the host does not need a microphone
q.question: What is the main advantage of recording the show with three cameras and choosing one feed at a time from the control room?
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) Different angles are captured and shown as people speak
Why: A multi-camera set-up covers the host, the guests and the audience at the same time, and the best shot is chosen as the talk unfolds.
Why not the others: (B) is wrong, since the case says the show was edited later. (C) and (D) are unrelated to the number of cameras.
Key point: Multi-camera production suits talk shows, news and sports.

q.sub_topic: The strip with each guest's name
q.question: The strip at the bottom of the screen showing each guest's name and title is called a:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lower third
Why: A lower third is a caption placed in the lower part of the screen to identify a speaker.
Why not the others: (A) is a line of moving text, often with headlines. (B) is a faint channel logo. (D) is a full-screen title.
Key point: Lower thirds are added as graphics in post-production.

q.sub_topic: Why Neha adds viewers' questions
options: A) It makes the show interactive and may draw younger viewers
B) It reduces the need to invite expert guests to the studio
C) It increases the show's length beyond half an hour
D) It allows the channel to stop measuring ratings
q.question: Which statement best explains Neha's decision to take viewers' questions from social media?
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) It makes the show interactive and may draw younger viewers
Why: The ratings showed few young viewers. Bringing in questions from social media, where younger people are active, makes the show two-way and gives them a reason to watch.
Why not the others: (B) is wrong, as the questions are put to the guests. (C) and (D) are not stated and do not follow.
Key point: Audience research guides changes to a programme.

q.sub_topic: Directions of communication in an organisation
q.targets: M1:upward communication, downward communication, horizontal communication peers, grapevine informal
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Type)
(A) Upward communication
(B) Downward communication
(C) Horizontal communication
(D) Grapevine

List-II (Example)
(I) A manager gives instructions to the staff
(II) Informal rumours passing among employees
(III) An employee sends a suggestion to the manager
(IV) Two heads of department discuss a joint plan
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Upward communication goes from staff to managers (III). Downward goes from managers to staff (I). Horizontal is between people at the same level (IV), and the grapevine is the informal rumour network (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps upward and downward. (B) swaps downward and horizontal. (D) swaps horizontal and grapevine.
Key point: Communication in groups and organisations flows in several directions.

q.sub_topic: Media and representation
q.targets: M1:representation shapes perception, stereotypes simplify, under representation rare
q.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The way the media represent a group can shape how people see that group.
(B) Stereotypes reduce a group to a few simple, repeated traits.
(C) Media representation is always a neutral mirror of reality.
(D) Under-representation means a group rarely appears in the media.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Representation shapes ideas about groups, stereotypes simplify, and under-representation leaves some groups almost invisible.
Why not the others: (C) is false. The media select and frame what they show, so representation is never simply neutral. Options (C) and (D) include (C), and (A) leaves out (D).
Key point: Representation is a construction, not a copy of reality.

q.sub_topic: Television in India from 1972 to 2004
q.targets: M1:bombay tv 1972, doordarshan separate 1976, cable act 1995, dd free dish 2004
q.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) A television centre opens in Bombay
(B) Doordarshan's free direct-to-home service begins
(C) Doordarshan is separated from All India Radio
(D) The Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act is passed
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Why: The Bombay centre opened in 1972, and Doordarshan was separated from AIR in 1976. The Cable Act was passed in 1995, and DD's free DTH service (now DD Free Dish) began in 2004.
Why not the others: (B) puts 1976 before 1972. (C) puts 1995 before 1976. (D) puts 2004 before 1995.
Key point: Indian TV grew from a few centres to cable and satellite.

q.sub_topic: Radio, TV and newspapers together
q.question: Radio, television and newspapers, which reach large audiences, are together called the mass ____.
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) media
Why: The mass media are the channels that carry messages to large audiences.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not complete the term.
Key point: Each mass medium uses technology to reach many people at once.

q.sub_topic: Turning a message into a signal
q.question: In Shannon and Weaver's model, the part that changes the message into a signal that can travel, such as a telephone mouthpiece, is the:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Transmitter
Why: The transmitter converts the message into a signal for the channel.
Why not the others: (A) turns the signal back into a message. (B) is the person who gets the message. (D) is where the message starts.
Key point: The model follows a message from source to destination through a channel.

q.sub_topic: McLuhan's hot and cool media
q.question: Marshall McLuhan called media that give a lot of detail and need little effort from the audience, such as radio and film, "hot". Media that need the audience to fill in more, such as the telephone, he called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cool media
Why: McLuhan divided media into hot (high detail, low participation) and cool (low detail, high participation).
Why not the others: (A) is not his term. (C) and (D) are other ways of grouping media.
Key point: McLuhan focused on how a medium itself affects the audience.

q.sub_topic: The reach of SITE
q.question: The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (1975–76) beamed programmes to about ____ villages in six states.
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2,400
Why: SITE reached about 2,400 villages in six states with programmes on farming, health and education.
Why not the others: (B) is too few, and (C) and (D) are far too many.
Key point: SITE showed that satellites could carry development messages.

q.sub_topic: Static on a radio set
q.question: Crackling static that makes a radio broadcast hard to hear is an example of:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Technical noise
Why: Technical (mechanical) noise comes from faults in the equipment or the channel, such as static.
Why not the others: (A) comes from the meaning of words. (B) comes from the listener's state of mind. (C) comes from cultural differences.
Key point: Noise can arise at any point between sender and receiver.

q.sub_topic: What is not a mass medium
options: A) A national daily newspaper with a wide circulation
C) A phone call between two friends
q.question: Mass media reach large, scattered audiences. Which of these does NOT count as mass media?
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) A phone call between two friends
Why: A phone call between two friends is interpersonal communication. It does not reach a large audience.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) reach large audiences, so they are mass media.
Key point: Mass media need a large, scattered audience.

q.sub_topic: Copy-editing marks
q.targets: M2:dele remove, caps capitals, trs transpose, run on no break
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Mark)
(A) dele
(B) caps
(C) trs
(D) run on

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Swap the order of two letters or words
(II) Set in capital letters
(III) Do not start a new paragraph here
(IV) Remove the marked text
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: "Dele" means delete (IV), "caps" means capitals (II), "trs" means transpose (I), and "run on" means continue without a break (III).
Why not the others: (B) swaps dele and caps. (C) swaps caps and trs. (D) swaps trs and run on.
Key point: Standard marks let editors and printers work without confusion.

q.sub_topic: Ethics of news photographs
q.targets: M2:no altering news photos, restraint graphic images, children photos care
q.question:
Consider the following statements about news photography:
(A) A news photo should not be digitally altered in a way that changes its meaning.
(B) Graphic images of dead or injured people should be used with restraint.
(C) Photos of children need special care for their privacy.
(D) Staging a news photo is acceptable if it looks real.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Altering meaning deceives readers, graphic images can hurt victims' families, and children need protection.
Why not the others: (D) is false. A staged news photo misleads readers, however real it looks. Options (B) and (C) include (D), and (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: A news photo must be a truthful record.

q.sub_topic: Media laws from 1957 to 2023
q.targets: M2:copyright act 1957 passed, contempt act 1971, it act 2000, dpdp act 2023
q.question:
Arrange the following laws in chronological order:
(A) Information Technology Act
(B) Digital Personal Data Protection Act
(C) Copyright Act
(D) Contempt of Courts Act
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: The Copyright Act was passed in 1957 and the Contempt of Courts Act in 1971. The IT Act followed in 2000, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023.
Why not the others: (A) puts 1971 before 1957. (B) puts 2000 before 1971. (D) puts 2023 before 2000.
Key point: Media law has grown to cover the digital world.

q.sub_topic: What a headline does
options: A) Name the writer of the story
B) Sum up the story and attract readers
C) Give the place and date of filing
D) Explain what a photograph shows
q.question: The main job of a headline is to:
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) Sum up the story and attract readers
Why: A headline sums up the main point in a few words and draws the reader in.
Why not the others: (A) is the byline. (C) is the dateline. (D) is the caption.
Key point: A headline must be short, accurate and striking.

q.sub_topic: A story no other paper has
q.question: An important story that one newspaper publishes before all its rivals is called a:
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) Scoop
Why: A scoop is an exclusive story that one outlet gets first.
Why not the others: (B) is a short item to fill space. (C) is a short news item. (D) gives new developments in an earlier story.
Key point: Scoops build a paper's reputation, but must still be verified.

q.sub_topic: A newspaper's archive of old stories
q.question: In newspaper slang, the library where old clippings, photos and background files are stored is called the:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Morgue
Why: The "morgue" is the newspaper's reference library of past stories.
Why not the others: (A) is where copy is edited. (B) is a branch office. (D) is a group of reporters sharing coverage.
Key point: Reporters use the archive for background and fact-checking.

q.sub_topic: The time by which copy must be filed
q.question: The latest time by which a reporter must file a story to make the next edition is called the ____.
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) deadline
Why: The deadline is the time limit for filing copy.
Why not the others: (A) gives the place and date of filing. (B) names the writer. (C) is a time before which a story must not be published.
Key point: Missing a deadline can mean a story misses the edition.

q.sub_topic: Speech that stirs hatred against a group
q.question: Speech or writing that stirs up hatred or violence against a group because of its religion, caste or race is called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) Hate speech
Why: Hate speech targets a group and incites hostility. The law restricts it in the interest of public order.
Why not the others: (A) uses humour to criticise. (C) uncovers hidden wrongdoing. (D) argues for a cause.
Key point: Free speech does not protect incitement to violence.

q.sub_topic: A wrongly matched newsroom job
options: A) Editor – in overall charge of the paper's content
B) Reporter – gathers and writes the news
C) Proofreader – writes the paper's editorials
D) Sub-editor – edits copy and writes headlines
q.question: In the newsroom pairs below, which job is wrongly described?
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Proofreader – writes the paper's editorials
Why: (C) is wrongly matched. A proofreader checks typeset pages for errors; editorials are written by senior editors.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correctly matched.
Key point: Each newsroom job has a defined role.

q.sub_topic: Measuring advertising
q.targets: M3:reach how many, frequency how often, impression one view, cpm cost per thousand
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Reach
(B) Frequency
(C) Impression
(D) CPM

List-II (Meaning)
(I) The cost of reaching one thousand people
(II) The number of different people who see an advertisement
(III) A single view of an advertisement
(IV) How many times a person sees an advertisement
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Reach counts different people (II). Frequency counts how often each sees it (IV). An impression is one view (III), and CPM is the cost per thousand (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps reach and frequency. (C) swaps frequency and impression. (D) swaps impression and CPM.
Key point: Media planners balance reach, frequency and cost.

q.sub_topic: Written tools of public relations
q.targets: M3:press release 5ws, media advisory invite, backgrounder context, press release not paid
q.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A press release should answer the main 5Ws.
(B) A press release is space bought in a newspaper.
(C) A media advisory invites journalists to an upcoming event.
(D) A backgrounder gives detailed context on an issue.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false. A press release is sent free to the media, which decide whether to use it; bought space is advertising.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: PR earns coverage; advertising buys it.

q.sub_topic: A free gift with a product
q.question: "Buy one toothpaste, get a toothbrush free" is an example of:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sales promotion
Why: Sales promotion uses short-term offers, such as gifts, discounts and contests, to boost sales.
Why not the others: (A) builds goodwill. (B) promotes a company's image. (D) influences lawmakers.
Key point: Sales promotion gives an immediate reason to buy.

q.sub_topic: Bernays and the engineering of consent
q.question: "The Engineering of Consent" (1947), an essay on planning communication to win public support, was written by:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Edward Bernays
Why: Edward Bernays wrote "The Engineering of Consent". He saw PR as a science of shaping public opinion.
Why not the others: (A) wrote the Declaration of Principles. (B) wrote Public Opinion. (C) wrote about media and the global village.
Key point: Bernays and Ivy Lee are the two founders of modern PR.

q.sub_topic: Advertising painted on village walls
q.question: Brand names and messages painted on the walls of houses and shops in villages are an example of:
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) Outdoor advertising
Why: Wall paintings are a cheap form of outdoor advertising, widely used to reach rural buyers.
Why not the others: (B) uses radio and TV. (C) uses the internet. (D) uses small text advertisements in papers.
Key point: Rural advertising uses local, low-cost media.

q.sub_topic: The person who writes an advertisement's words
q.question: In an advertising agency, the person who writes the words of an advertisement is called a ____.
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) copywriter
Why: The copywriter writes the headline, text and slogans.
Why not the others: (A) designs the visuals. (C) chooses the media. (D) handles the client.
Key point: The copywriter and art director form the creative team.

q.sub_topic: Riding on an event without sponsoring it
q.question: A brand that is not an official sponsor runs advertisements during a big cricket tournament that make people think it is linked to the event. This is called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ambush marketing
Why: Ambush marketing links a brand with an event without paying to sponsor it.
Why not the others: (A) shares costs between two advertisers. (B) promotes a company's image. (D) promotes social causes.
Key point: Event organisers try to protect their official sponsors from ambush marketing.

q.sub_topic: Services of All India Radio
q.targets: M5:vividh bharati entertainment, external services abroad, news services division bulletins, fm rainbow urban music
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Service)
(A) Vividh Bharati
(B) External Services Division
(C) News Services Division
(D) FM Rainbow

List-II (Purpose)
(I) Light entertainment, film music and plays
(II) Music and lifestyle programmes for city listeners on FM
(III) Programmes for listeners in other countries
(IV) Preparing and broadcasting news bulletins
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Vividh Bharati offers entertainment (I). The External Services reach listeners abroad (III). The News Services Division prepares bulletins (IV), and FM Rainbow serves city listeners (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps Vividh Bharati and External Services. (B) swaps External and News Services. (C) swaps News Services and FM Rainbow.
Key point: AIR runs separate services for different audiences.

q.sub_topic: Interviewing on radio
q.targets: M5:open ended questions, avoid verbal nods, research guest
q.question:
Consider the following statements about radio interviews:
(A) Open-ended questions get fuller answers than yes-or-no questions.
(B) The interviewer should avoid saying "uh-huh" while the guest speaks.
(C) Questions should be long and contain several parts.
(D) The interviewer should research the guest beforehand.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false. Long, many-part questions confuse guests and listeners; one short question at a time works best.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are correct. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: Good interviews come from preparation and simple questions.

q.sub_topic: An advertisement on radio
q.question: A short advertisement broadcast on radio is commonly called a radio:
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) Spot
Why: Radio advertisements are sold as spots, usually 10 to 60 seconds long.
Why not the others: (B) is an online or printed strip. (C) is an outdoor board. (D) is a sheet placed inside a newspaper.
Key point: Spots are priced by length and time of day.

q.sub_topic: How a radio script is typed
options: A) They look neater when filed in the station's library
B) Listeners can ask for copies and read them later
C) The presenter can read them easily and mark changes
D) They can be reprinted in newspapers without retyping
q.question: Radio scripts are typed in double spacing with wide margins mainly so that:
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) The presenter can read them easily and mark changes
Why: Spacing and margins make the script easy to read aloud and leave room for last-minute changes and marks.
Why not the others: (A) is not a purpose. (B) and (D) are wrong, since scripts are for the presenter, not the public.
Key point: A radio script is a working tool for reading aloud.

q.sub_topic: A vehicle for live broadcasts outside the studio
q.question: A vehicle fitted with equipment to broadcast live from places such as a stadium or a festival is called an:
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) OB van
Why: An outside broadcast (OB) van carries the equipment needed to broadcast live away from the studio.
Why not the others: (B) is a room for editing. (C) is inside the studio building. (D) stores old recordings.
Key point: OB vans bring live events to listeners and viewers.

q.sub_topic: Film awards and festivals in India
q.targets: M6:phalke award lifetime, national film awards government, iffi goa festival, filmfare magazine
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Award or event)
(A) Dadasaheb Phalke Award
(B) National Film Awards
(C) IFFI
(D) Filmfare Awards

List-II (Description)
(I) An international film festival held in Goa
(II) Awards given by a film magazine
(III) Awards given by the Government of India for films of the year
(IV) India's highest award for lifetime contribution to cinema
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: The Phalke Award honours lifetime contribution (IV). The National Film Awards are given by the government (III). IFFI is held in Goa (I), and the Filmfare Awards come from a magazine (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the Phalke Award and the National Awards. (B) swaps the National Awards and IFFI. (D) swaps IFFI and Filmfare.
Key point: Awards and festivals help films find recognition and audiences.

q.sub_topic: People and papers on a film shoot
q.targets: M6:line producer budget daily, call sheet schedule, continuity errors
q.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The editor decides the budget of a film.
(B) A line producer manages the day-to-day budget and schedule of a shoot.
(C) A call sheet tells the cast and crew when and where to report.
(D) A continuity error occurs when details change between shots of one scene.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: (B), (C) and (D) are correct. The line producer runs the shoot's budget and schedule, the call sheet sets each day's reporting, and continuity errors are mismatches between shots.
Why not the others: (A) is false. The budget is set by the producer; the editor assembles the footage. Options (A) and (B) include (A), and (C) leaves out (C).
Key point: A shoot is run on budgets, schedules and careful records.

q.sub_topic: Tasks in the order a film is made
q.targets: M6:development securing rights, casting pre production, principal photography, colour grading post
q.question:
Arrange the following tasks in the order in which they are done when making a film:
(A) Principal photography
(B) Securing the rights to a novel
(C) Colour grading the footage
(D) Casting the actors
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Rights are secured in development, actors are cast in pre-production, principal photography is the production stage, and colour grading is post-production.
Why not the others: (A) casts before the project is secured. (C) shoots before casting. (D) grades before shooting.
Key point: A film moves from development to pre-production, production and post-production.

q.sub_topic: The person in creative charge of a film
q.question: The person who has overall creative control of a film and guides the actors and camera is the:
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) Director
Why: The director shapes the film's creative vision.
Why not the others: (B) arranges money and manages the project. (C) supplies the film to cinemas. (D) screens it.
Key point: The producer runs the business; the director runs the creative side.

q.sub_topic: Why separate pictures seem to move
q.question: The eye's tendency to hold an image for a fraction of a second, so that a series of still frames appears as continuous movement, is called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Persistence of vision
Why: Persistence of vision was the idea behind early moving pictures: rapidly shown stills blend into motion.
Why not the others: (A) is how much of a shot is in focus. (B) is the shape of the frame. (C) is how many frames are shown each second.
Key point: Early experiments in cinema built on this effect.

q.sub_topic: The director of the Apu Trilogy
q.question: Pather Panchali, Aparajito and Apur Sansar together form the Apu Trilogy, directed by ____.
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Satyajit Ray
Why: Satyajit Ray made the Apu Trilogy between 1955 and 1959.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) were other important Indian directors of the period.
Key point: The trilogy brought Indian realist cinema to world attention.

q.sub_topic: Platforms and their kinds
q.targets: M7:reddit forum, quora q and a, telegram messaging channels, wikipedia wiki collaborative
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Platform)
(A) Reddit
(B) Quora
(C) Telegram
(D) Wikipedia

List-II (Kind)
(I) A question-and-answer site
(II) A discussion forum divided into communities
(III) A messaging app with broadcast channels
(IV) An encyclopaedia written jointly by users
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Reddit is a discussion forum (II). Quora is a question-and-answer site (I). Telegram is a messaging app with channels (III), and Wikipedia is a jointly written encyclopaedia (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps Reddit and Quora. (C) swaps Quora and Telegram. (D) swaps Telegram and Wikipedia.
Key point: Social media includes forums, wikis and messaging, not only networking sites.

q.sub_topic: Filing a complaint on the cyber crime portal
q.question:
Arrange the following steps of filing a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in in the correct order:
(A) Upload screenshots and other evidence
(B) Note the acknowledgement number for follow-up
(C) Register with a mobile number and log in
(D) Fill in the details of the incident
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: The user registers and logs in, describes the incident, uploads evidence, and then receives an acknowledgement number.
Why not the others: (A) fills in details before logging in. (B) uploads evidence before describing the incident. (D) gets the acknowledgement before uploading evidence.
Key point: Keeping evidence and the acknowledgement number helps follow-up.

q.sub_topic: Sites such as Facebook and Instagram
q.question: Facebook and Instagram, where users build profiles and connect with friends, are called social ____ sites.
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) networking
Why: Social networking sites let users create profiles and connect with others.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not describe these platforms.
Key point: Networking sites are built around connections between users.

q.sub_topic: Publishing someone's private details online
q.question: Publishing a person's home address, phone number or other private details online to harass them is called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Doxxing
Why: Doxxing exposes private information so that others can target the victim.
Why not the others: (A) tricks people into giving information. (B) sends unwanted bulk messages. (C) provokes people with offensive posts.
Key point: Never share others' private details online.

q.sub_topic: An unsafe habit online
options: A) Using strong, different passwords for each account
C) Sharing an OTP with a caller from "the bank"
D) Keeping apps and software updated
q.question: Which of the following is NOT a safe practice online?
q.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sharing an OTP with a caller from "the bank"
Why: Banks never ask for OTPs. Sharing one lets fraudsters take money from the account.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) all improve online safety.
Key point: An OTP is for the account holder alone.

q.sub_topic: Problems of the information age
q.targets: M8:filter bubble algorithm, infodemic crisis flood, digital literacy skills, information overload
q.question:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Term)
(A) Filter bubble
(B) Infodemic
(C) Digital literacy
(D) Information overload

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Having more information than one can take in
(II) A flood of true and false information during a crisis
(III) A personalised feed that shows only what a user already likes
(IV) The skills to use and judge digital media
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: A filter bubble is a personalised feed (III). An infodemic is a flood of information in a crisis (II). Digital literacy is the skill to judge digital media (IV), and information overload is having too much information (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps filter bubble and infodemic. (C) swaps infodemic and digital literacy. (D) swaps digital literacy and information overload.
Key point: New media brings plenty of information but also new problems.

q.sub_topic: Artificial intelligence in the newsroom
q.targets: M8:ai writes simple reports, ai images misinformation, label ai content
q.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) AI tools can write simple reports such as match scores and results.
(B) AI-generated images can be used to spread misinformation.
(C) Newsrooms should label content made with AI.
(D) AI has removed the need for human verification of news.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
q.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false. AI can make mistakes and invent facts, so human checking is still essential.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are correct. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a correct statement as false.
Key point: AI is a tool for journalists, not a replacement for verification.

q.sub_topic: Playing media without a full download
q.question: Watching a video or listening to music over the internet as it plays, without first downloading the whole file, is called:
q.explanation:
Answer: (D) Streaming
Why: Streaming sends the media in a continuous flow, so it can be played as it arrives.
Why not the others: (A) sends files to a server. (B) stores content. (C) produces paper copies.
Key point: Streaming made OTT services and podcasts popular.

q.sub_topic: An app that collects news from many sources
q.question: An app that gathers stories from many news websites and shows them in one place is called a news:
q.explanation:
Answer: (B) Aggregator
Why: A news aggregator collects and displays stories from many sources, often using algorithms.
Why not the others: (A) gathers and sells news it reports itself. (C) is a news office in a city. (D) sells features and columns to many papers.
Key point: Aggregators change how readers find news.

passages.M4:
Neha produces "Seedha Sawaal", a weekly half-hour talk show on a regional news channel. This week's topic is the city's water shortage. On Monday her team researches the issue, books a municipal engineer, a resident-welfare leader and a hydrologist as guests, and writes a rundown that lists each segment with its exact timing.

The show is recorded on Thursday in a studio with three cameras and a small live audience. From the control room, one camera feed at a time is chosen and sent to the recording, so that the host, a guest or the audience can be shown as each one speaks. In editing, the programme is cut to 22 minutes to leave room for advertisements, and each guest's name and title are added in a strip at the bottom of the screen when they first appear.

A month later, the ratings show that the show is watched mostly by people over 45. Neha starts taking viewers' questions from the channel's social media pages and putting them to the guests during the show.
